matters.title: B. Approval of an agreement with BenTek, Inc. for Employee Benefits Enrollment and Administration Software and associated services for a term of three (3) years with a monthly fee of $4.64 per employee per month with a projected annual expenditure of $61,776.
matters.body: Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting
matters.text:
Agenda Item Details 

 Meeting 
 Sep 10, 2024 - Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting 
 Category 
 5. Consent (Automatic Approval) Agenda - This agenda consists of ministerial or “housekeeping” items required by law such as routine bids, contracts, purchases, and resolutions. Items may be removed from the consent agenda for separate consideration at the request of two Councilmembers. 
 Subject 
 B. Approval of an agreement with BenTek, Inc. for Employee Benefits Enrollment and Administration Software and associated services for a term of three (3) years with a monthly fee of $4.64 per employee per month with a projected annual expenditure of $61,776. 
 Type 
 Action (Consent) 
 Preferred Date 
 Sep 10, 2024 
 Absolute Date 
 Sep 17, 2024 
 Fiscal Impact 
 Yes 
 Dollar Amount 
 185,328.00 
 Budgeted 
 Yes 
 Budget Source 
 Self-Insurance Fund 
 Goals 

 Quality of Life 

 Summary: 
 The City Council awarded a three (3) year agreement to BenTek, Inc. in Fiscal Year (FY) 2021 for an online benefit enrollment and administration software system and associated services for a monthly fee of $4.64 per employee per month. The annual expenditure for the software and services has been $54,733.44 since the FY2021 approval. 

 Since the City’s implementation of BenTek in FY2018, the use of web-based technology for self-serve benefits enrollment and benefits administration has continued to increase in popularity. BenTek, Inc. has continued to add to its many features made available each year, and serves as a one-stop shop for employees and families to learn about their benefits and take action. Using the dedicated website, employees are guided through the process of selecting the benefits they wish to elect either at the time of hire, when a qualifying life event (e.g., marriage, divorce, birth of a child) occurs, or during the City’s annual open enrollment period. After approval by Risk Management staff, the data automatically updates in the payroll system and benefit vendor files, thus minimizing data entry. Staff is able to define eligibility criteria; therefore, employees are only presented with benefits and plan options for which they are eligible. BenTek, Inc. provides tracking and reporting features allowing staff to monitor progress of each employee throughout the enrollment process. 

 Prior to implementing BenTek in 2018, Risk Management staff consulted with IT to procure a software system that integrates with the City’s Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system (i.e. CentralSquare). BenTek, Inc. is a preferred provider for CentralSquare. 

 Multiple benefits exist for continuing the use of an online enrollment system: 

 Time savings 
 Increased efficiency in reviewing and approving elections 
 Automated migration of enrollment data to benefit vendor portals and to the City’s payroll system through electronic data interface 
 Reduced benefit vendor and payroll reconciliations due to data entry errors 
 Reduced costs and by “going green” 
 Eliminates the need for paper, printing, and postage for open enrollment packets 
 Reduces staff time spent assembling and distributing paper enrollment packets 
 Improved Service to Employees 
 Dedicated website accessible anytime by employees and their dependents 
 Convenient access to benefit plan information and options 
 Allows employees to review options with dependents and make a joint decision most appropriate to their family needs 
 Allows employees the opportunity to review benefit elections, including assigned beneficiaries and dependents, throughout the year 
 Allows employees the ability to submit qualifying life event changes and supporting documents from the convenience of home or office 

 The expiring agreement ($54,733) allowed for a three percent (3%) fee increase. In addition, the City's current number of benefit eligible lives (1051) has increased. On a per employee per month basis (PEPM at $4.64), along with the 3% increase, the proposed annual fee is $60,275.28. In addition, and in the event the City makes any insurance carrier changes during the life of the agreement, there will be a $1,500 fee to set up new file feeds resulting in a projected annual expenditure of $61,776. 

 BentTek, Inc. remains the preferred provider for electronic employee benefits enrollment and management software that directly interfaces with CentralSquare HTE/Naviline, the City’s Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) software. BenTek, Inc. has provided exceptional customer service and additional features during the current agreement period. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Staff respectfully requests the City Council approve an agreement with BenTek, Inc. for employee benefits enrollment and administration software and associated services for a term of three (3) years with a monthly fee of $4.64 per employee per month. The projected annual expenditure is $61,776 with the remaining two (2) years being the same. 

 Options: 
 Approve an agreement with BenTek, Inc. for Employee Benefits Enrollment and Administration software and services for a term of three (3) years with a monthly fee of $4.64 per employee per month and a $1,500 allowance for possible new file feeds, for a projected annual expenditure of $61,776. 
 Do not approve an agreement with BenTek, Inc. and provide direction to staff. With the City’s annual open enrollment period scheduled for October, this could leave the City without an online benefit portal. 

 Attachments: 
 1. CentralSquare preferred vendor statement
 2. BenTek Master Software Agreement & Professional Services Agreement

matters.title: D. Approval of a professional services contract for Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition Evaluation with Concentric Integration in the not to exceed amount of $192,100
matters.body: Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting
matters.text:

 Meeting 
 May 14, 2024 - Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting 
 Category 
 5. Consent (Automatic Approval) Agenda - This agenda consists of ministerial or “housekeeping” items required by law such as routine bids, contracts, purchases, and resolutions. Items may be removed from the consent agenda for separate consideration at the request of two Councilmembers. 
 Subject 
 D. Approval of a professional services contract for Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition Evaluation with Concentric Integration in the not to exceed amount of $192,100 
 Type 
 Action (Consent) 
 Preferred Date 
 May 14, 2024 
 Absolute Date 
 May 14, 2024 
 Fiscal Impact 
 Yes 
 Dollar Amount 
 192,100.00 
 Budgeted 
 Yes 
 Budget Source 
 Water Fund 
 Goals 

 Service 

 Infrastructure 

 Summary: 

 Water Services requests City Council consideration and approval of a contract with Concentric Integration in the not to exceed amount of $192,100 allowing for engineering services to the Water SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) system. For this contract, the term “SCADA system” encompasses the computers, instrumentation and metering, control strategy, and software to monitor, control, and analyze equipment used for production, storage, treatment, and delivery of drinking water to the end-user. 

 The presented contract includes two tasks: (1) Evaluation and Condition Assessment of the Water SCADA system, and (2) Development of Automation, Control, and Monitoring to the Wickson Creek Water Interconnection Station. 

 Task 1 - Evaluation and Condition Assessment 

 The Water SCADA system is aged. Much of the system’s components are approaching end of life or are no longer commercially available by the manufacturer. Upgrading the equipment will ensure market availability of service and parts in the event of component failure and/or system expansion. A second driver for upgrade centers on the current control strategy’s limited automation and inability to function independent of operator input. Redeveloping the control strategy for full automation will allow computer control (automation) of routine system operations and free employees to refocus attention to other needs. 

 The success of the control strategy to achieve the automation goal is dependent upon having the correct configuration and instrumentation installed at each remote site. The instrumentation type, communication protocol, control panel, and monitored points of each remote site must be compatible with the developed control strategy or the desired function may not be achieved. Through this task, Concentric will inventory all aspects of the Water SCADA system to understand operability and maintainability issues and explore opportunities for improvement and expansion. Concentric will inventory the processors, hardware, instrumentation, and control strategies, and then will recommend changes, continuation, upgrade, and/or replacements where appropriate. The product of this work will result in written condition assessment for the Water SCADA system, development of a cost estimation for system upgrade, and a recommended plan of work for system upgrade. The information provided in the condition assessment will be used to establish a construction contract for consideration by City Council at a future date. 

 The cost of this service is $98,500. 

 Task 2 - Wickson Creek Water Interconnection 

 This station serves as an interconnection point between the Bryan Public Water System and Wickson Creek Special Utility District. Concentric will establish automation to the station outside of the Water SCADA. Taking this standalone approach will significantly simplify the project by avoiding software and hardware challenges and incompatibility anticipated by adding new assets and command scripts into older version software and programming. Secondly, performing this work outside of the Water SCADA ensures no unintended loss of system control results during programming and integration of the added station. 

 Work performed in this task include: (1) installation of a new master control panel and Human Machine Interface at the operations building; (2) installation of a new control panel and associated hardware at the interconnect station; and (3) purchase and programming of software and control strategy for the station. Hardware and software procured in this task will be reused as part of the future upgrade to the Water SCADA system. At that time, the standalone approach will be decommissioned and integrated into the Water SCADA system. 

 The cost of this service is $93,600. 

 Concentric Integration was selected for this project through response and participation in Request for Qualification #23-019. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 Staff recommends award of a professional services contract with Concentric Integration. The work performed through this contract will provide essential planning for future upgrade of the Water SCADA system and establish necessary control and monitoring to the Wickson Creek Interconnection Station. 

 Options: 

 1. Approve the purchase. 

 2. Do not approve the purchase and provide direction. 

 Attachments: 

 1. Contract

 Summary: 

 On November 15, 2022, the City of Bryan (Landlord) entered into a Ground Lease Agreement with SMBG Bryan, LLC (Tenant) to develop the Schulman's Movie Bowl Grille on 5.644 acres of land in the Travis Bryan Midtown Park (Property). The Tenant has entered into a $26.6 MM Builder and Mechanic's Lien contract (Mechanic's Lien) with Bartlett Cocke General Contractors, LLC (Contractor) to construct improvements on the Property. However, construction of the improvements cannot commence until a Transfer, as defined in Article XXI of the Ground Lease Agreement, is first approved by the Landlord.

 The Tenant is requesting that the Landlord give its consent to the Tenant to grant the Mechanic's Lien upon Tenant's interest in the Lease, which secures the Tenant's obligations with the Contractor. Currently, the Tenant is finalizing terms and documentation on the construction loan (loan) that will provide financing to complete the project. The Mechanic's Lien is one of the final components to completing the loan. Upon closing on the loan, the Contractor will assign the Mechanic's Lien to the lending institution. The Tenant will then provide to the lending institution a deed of trust to secure the loan.

 The leasehold deed of trust requires consent of the Landlord. Upon consent approval by the Landlord, the Mechanic's Lien will be assigned to the lending institution, thus allowing it to have first priority in the event of a default by the Tenant.

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 Staff recommends consenting to the Mechanic's Lien to allow the tenant the ability to begin construction on the Schulman's Movie Bowl Grille project.

 Options: 

 1. Approve consent to the Mechanic's Lien

 2. Do not approve consent to the Mechanic's Lein

 Type

 Budget Source

 Goals

 Summary: 

 Water Services respectfully requests City Council’s approval for factory reconditioning of two belt filter presses with Alfa Laval in the not to exceed amount of $522,371. Sludge dewatering is a regulatory requirement incorporated into the City’s wastewater discharge permit; Water Services utilizes the belt filter press to satisfy this requirement. Alfa Laval serves as the original equipment manufacturer for both filter presses and omits the necessity for competitive bidding for this service. Many of the parts used in this project are proprietary and only available from Alfa Laval. Services performed in this purchase will factory recondition two identical belt filter press machines. 

 Sludge dewatering involves transforming "sludge slurry" (liquid phase) into a “sludge cake” (solid phase). The belt press uses a combination of pressure and surface area to remove water from raw liquid sludge. The sludge slurry is chemically conditioned and then sandwiched between two tensioned porous belts and is passed over and under rollers of various diameters to squeeze out excess liquid and produce a sludge cake. The services performed in this contract will factory recondition both machines with new parts and components. Both filter presses were installed as part of Capital Improvement Project 411-893 and are approaching 33 years in age. Obsolete parts are no longer available and will be replaced with "today's technology". This service will replace the drive motor, hydraulic tensioning system, rollers, bearing housing, wash boxes, rotating mechanisms, and safety mechanisms with factory new replacements. 

 These machines provide 100% duty for their respective plant. Loss of operation of either filter press will result in an "end of chain" failure because there is no installed redundancy for either machine. Both presses have reached an operational point where they should be reconditioned or replaced with new. Staff has considered both options and feels reconditioning presents the best return on investment. Reconditioning is approximately half the cost of purchasing a complete new machine and does not require hiring of an engineer and general contractor for demolition and installation. Secondly, reconditioning is completed in-place and omits the need to remove the roof and support structure of both dewatering buildings to accommodate work. 

 Staff believes factory reconditioning will provide a comparative level of operational life and performance when compared to purchase of a new machine. Performed work will be warrantied for one year. All parts and components used in the reconditioning process will be factory new and compatible with the manufacturer’s new build design. This process is value added by replacing end of life and obsolete parts and components with new, which are market available and manufacturer supported. 

 Note: reconditioning of the Burton Creek press has a price difference of $4,651 compared to the Still Creek press. This difference is the result of additional parts required to repair the sludge feed chute and associated mounting angles. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 Staff recommends the City Council award a contract to Alfa Laval allowing factory reconditioning of two belt filter presses in the not to exceed amount of $522,371. 

 Options: 

 1. Approve purchase. 

 2. Do not approve purchase and provide direction. 

 Attachments: 

 1. Contract

 Summary: 

 The City’s approved budget plan calls for the issuance of bonds to fund approximately $48,215,000 of capital improvements for Fiscal Years 2024 and 2025. On January 9, 2024, the City of Bryan City Council approved the publication of Notice of Intent to issue the certificates of obligation (COs). In compliance with State law, notice was published in the Bryan-College Station Eagle on January 18, 2024, and again on January 25, 2024, and has been posted on the City's website. The City Council now has an opportunity to approve an ordinance authorizing the issuance of combination tax and revenue certificates of obligation consistent with that notice.

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 This bond issuance provides funding to support the City's approved Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) program with the current tax rate. City staff recommends approving the ordinance to issue the bonds.

 Summary: 

 In 2019, the City of Bryan adopted a Drought Contingency Plan as required by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), while also satisfying Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) requirements. The Drought Contingency Plan has several sections: A) Introduction, B) Authorization, C) Application, D) Definitions, E) Trigger Conditions, F) Notification and Public Education, G) Drought Response Stages, H) Variances, I) Wholesale Agreements/Contracts Provision, J) Enforcement, and K) Severability. 

 The overall purpose of the Drought Contingency Plan is to define a set of trigger points based off water system production abilities that enact stages of water restrictions designed to protect water system integrity. Triggers are targeted based on a percentage of production capability as measured against user demand. Although typically enacted during periods of extended drought, when user demand strains production ability, the Plan also can be enacted if production facilities lose capacity (e.g., equipment failure). The Plan details how to enact/rescind restrictions and works in conjunction with the Water Conservation Plan. TCEQ requires this Plan be updated at least every five years. The Plan was last approved in May 2019. 

 Staff recommends the City Council approve the ordinance changes to section 26 of the Code of Ordinances adopting the updated Drought Contingency Plan for May 2024. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 The Drought Contingency Plan establishes goals, strategies, and triggers to help protect the water system under conditions of extreme duress. Approval of the Plan also helps keep the water system in compliance with TCEQ regulations. The Drought Contingency Plan will prompt mandatory water restrictions, if trigger point thresholds are met. 

 Staff recommends approval of the ordinance changes and adopting the revised Drought Contingency Plan to be in effect from May 2024 to May 2029. The City has the option to revise the Plan before May 2029 should new water conservation strategies be identified and need to be incorporated. 

 Options: 

 Adopt the ordinance changes as presented. 

 Modify the Drought Contingency Plan and adopt the ordinance changes, which may require consideration at a future City Council meeting. 

 Provide direction to staff.

 Summary: 

 Thompsons Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant (Thompsons Creek) provides sewer service to Bryan’s west side. The plant commenced operation in May 2013. Thompsons Creek is constructed to treat an annual average flow of 2.0 million gallons per day (MGD) and is presently treating a little more than 1 MGD. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) requires permittees to initiate engineering and financial planning for plant expansion when the daily treated volume reaches 75% of the permitted annual average flow (1.5 MGD) for three consecutive months, and then begin construction of the expansion when the daily treated volume reaches 90% of the permitted annual average flow (1.9 MGD) for three consecutive months. 

 Significant growth is expected for the Thompsons Creek Sewer Basin in the near future. Annexation has vastly expanded the City’s land footprint in west Bryan. The incorporation of Texas A&M University RELLIS Campus and surrounding land into Bryan opens the door for development opportunity in this area. 

 Future plant expansion was incorporated into Thompsons Creek's original design. This is value-added by minimizing outages and other disruptions needed to accommodate the addition of equipment, tanks, and piping into the plant's layout and operation. This foresight also was placed in permitting. Thompsons Creek's discharge permit presently authorizes expansion of the plant to a final build capacity of 4.0 MGD (doubling its current size). Securing this approval in the discharge permit greatly reduces time spent in regulatory review and coordination for plant expansion. 

 The presented contract serves as the first step in addressing the future capacity needs of the plant and allowing design of the 2.0 MGD expansion, applications engineering for automation and control, and bidding services for advertisement of the construction project. The presented contract also satisfies regulatory coordination with TCEQ for permitting. In addition to designing the plant expansion, the scope includes modifying the discharge permit from 4.0 MGD to 8.0 MGD to accommodate future growth anticipated in the corridor. 

 CDM Smith (CDM) is the original design engineer for Thompsons Creek WWTP. CDM's expertise and familiarity with Thompsons Creek is value added for this project. A breakdown of deliverables is listed below: 

 Task 1: Project Management $108,000

 Task 2: Preliminary Investigations $34,000 

 Task 3: Design Phase $1,803,000

 Task 4: Bid Phase $48,000

 Task 5: Time and Materials $835,000

 Task 6: Additional Services $495,000 

 Total $3,323,000 

 Funding for this project will come from the Wastewater Fund.

 Water Services recommends the City Council award a professional services contract to CDM Smith, Inc. for design of expansion of Thompsons Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant in the not to exceed amount of $3,323,000. Added capacity to the plant is needed to meet future sewer needs of the sewer basin. The presented contract will satisfy the project design and regulatory elements required by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for this project.

 Summary: 
 Water Services respectfully requests the City Council’s approval of a contract with Teal Services LLC (Anderson, Texas) for construction services provided to Still Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant and Grease Plant in the not to exceed amount of $6,061,300. The improvements to be made address capacity concerns, replace aged equipment with new, and streamline operations through programmed automation. On June 19, 2024, Request for Bid (RFB) #24-041 was opened for the this project. The bid submitted by Teal Services represents the only bid received for this project. CDM Smith (CDM) is the design engineer for this project, and their recommendation of award is attached to this request. 

 A summary of each improvement is provided below: 

 Grease Plant 
 The Grease Plant (Still Creek Liquid Waste Processing Facility) serves as a regional disposal site for hauled liquid wastes. Grease traps are used by restaurants to limit fats, oil, and grease from entering the sanitary sewer. The trapped grease and solids are pumped and transported by a vacuum truck to a disposal site for processing. The Grease Plant was constructed in 2003 and currently provides service to 23 liquid waste hauling companies. Customers are billed based upon the waste volume and type transported. The Grease Plant is a net positive operation. 

 The site’s pumps, tanks, and other equipment have reached the end of life and require replacement. The proposed contract will replace the storage tanks, pumps, and piping with new components. Scheduled improvements go a step further by adding a recirculation system for blending of stored contents and installation of a mechanical press and conveyor to replace the use of gravity filter boxes for sludge dewatering. 

 Gravity filtration is labor dependent, time consuming, and inefficient for this process because grease binds to the filter cloth, which inhibits drainage. The mechanical press dewaters using a flocculation tank where polymer is mixed into the grease solution. The flocculated waste is then fed to a drum auger that conveys the waste through a series of concentric rings that taper in diameter as the waste travels the length of the auger. Pressure is used to squeeze water from the processed sludge. The resulting sludge is landfill ready and requires no additional processing. A conveyor is used to load the dried sludge into a transport container for disposal. Improvement to the dewatering process is expected to reduce offsite odors by minimizing the amount of time sludge is held onsite for processing. The mechanical press is able to operate without human involvement because of programmed automation. This process frees up staff to rededicate attention to other needs in plant. 

 Digester Conversion 
 Still Creek is currently outfitted with anaerobic digestion. The digesters stabilize the waste solids through microbial decomposition under anaerobic conditions (i.e., without oxygen). The digester system is in need of repair for continued operation. Without repair, the likelihood of failure to the system increases with passing time. Example failures include seal failures, stoppages/obstructions, or damage to the digester lids. A critical failure would impact the plant's ability to process sludge and threaten the plant 's ability to meet its discharge permit. 

 Anaerobic systems are difficult to operate and carry a higher price tag to rehabilitate compared to converting the process to an aerobic system (i.e., with oxygen). Staff evaluated both options and found aerobic conversion to be best-fit. Water Services took a similar position in 2018 when Burton Creek WWTP’s anaerobic digester was converted to aerobic. Aerobic systems are generally easier to operate and provide an added benefit in odor reduction because the waste is aerated. Consequently, a erobic systems have a higher operational cost because diffused oxygen must be introduced constantly to the system. 

 The presented contract allows for demolition of the digester floating lid, evacuation of contained waste, demolition of sludge transfer and gas piping, and installation of new blower pad and motor control center. 

 Bar Screen 
 The bar screen removes objects such as rags, plastics, and other larger debris from entering the treatment plant. Screening is accomplished through a series of vertical bars that allow water to pass through while stopping big objects, which are removed by a mechanical screening rake. Wear and damage to the bar rack from years of operation have created gaps and pinch points in the bar spacing that allow pass through of rags and debris. The existing bar screen is a single rake model prone to misalignment with the rake's teeth and the bar channels. The bar screen's poor performance is felt in the intermediate pump station that routinely becomes overloaded with rags and debris. Intermediate pump performance drops considerably after a rain event when peaking flows are received. Pumps impacted by foreign objects must be removed from service and cleaned. 

 The bar screen will be replaced with a multi-rake screen to provide faster cycle times for removal of entrapped debris from the bar rack. Unlike the existing screen, the proposed screen's rakes are integrated into a track affixed to the bar rack. This design keeps the rake's teeth in contact with the screen's bar - ensuring spacing of the bars remains true throughout the life of the screen. The same screen approach was implemented at Burton Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant in 2019 when its single rake bar screen was replaced with a multi-rake. Pumping issues experienced in Burton Creek's intermediate pump station ceased after installation of the multi-rake system. The same success is expected for Still Creek's installation. 

 Funding for this project is from the Wastewater Fund with a reimbursement resolution from future debt. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Water Services recommends the City Council award the contract with Teal Services LLC in the not to exceed amount of $6,061,300 allowing upgrades made to Still Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant and Grease Plant. The improvements performed in the contract are needed to replace aging equipment, minimize risk for service loss or interruption, and improve site operations.

 1. Approve the proposed contract. 
 2. Do not approve the proposed contract and provide staff direction.

In addition, this contract will include repairs and repaving of a parking lot at BTU’s Lake Bryan. 

 The Street Maintenance contract consists of forty-six (46) streets (or ~26 lane miles) receiving substantial pavement repairs followed by an overlay of asphalt, with eleven (11) of these streets totally reconstructed. The scope of work includes the construction of an engineered vertical retaining wall, two new ADA parking spaces, an ADA access route to the bathhouse, and pavement markings.  Four (4) competitive bids were received and opened on May 22, 2024. Brazos Paving Inc. (BPI) submitted the low bid at $4,364,372.50, representing the best value to the City.  Subject 
 D. Rezoning Request Case No. RZ24-12 - Public hearing, presentation, and consideration of the first and only reading of an ordinance of the City of Bryan, Texas, amending Chapter 130, Zoning, of the Bryan Code of Ordinances, by changing the zoning classification from a combination of Agricultural – Open District (A-O) and Residential District – 5000 (RD-5) to Commercial District (C-3) on 39 properties, being 52.82 acres of land in three clusters generally adjoining the northwest and southeast sides of East State Highway 21 between North Earl Rudder Freeway (SH 6) and Old Kurten Road, North Thornberry Drive and Wallis Road, and at its intersection with Crosswind Drive in Bryan Brazos County, Texas 
 Type 
 Action 
 Preferred Date 
 Jun 18, 2024 
 Absolute Date 
 Jun 18, 2024 
 Fiscal Impact 
 No 
 Budgeted 
 No 
 Goals 

 Quality of Life 

 Infrastructure 

 Economic Development 

 Summary: 

 As part of the Planning and Zoning Commission’s 2024 Plan of Work, the Commission identified the necessity to study growth and development patterns within the City to ensure current zoning designations align with the currently adopted Comprehensive Plan (Blueprint 2040), as well as the needs and aspirations of Bryan’s residents and businesses. Late last year, the Planning and Zoning Commission moved forward with an assessment of the current growth and development patterns to determine where City-initiated rezonings may be appropriate. The City was divided into several sections to examine the abovementioned trends, and the East State Highway 21 corridor was selected as an appropriate location to start due to recent development trends and approved rezoning requests that have occurred in the area. 

 The Planning and Zoning Commission proposes to change the zoning classification on several properties located along the East State Highway 21 corridor from a combination of Agricultural – Open District (A-O) and Residential District – 5000 (RD-5) to Commercial District (C-3). A total of thirty-nine (39) lots are proposed to be rezoned to Commercial District (C-3), of which thirty-one (31) are currently zoned A-O District and eight (8) are zoned RD-5 District. These properties total 52.82 acres of land within three (3) clusters generally adjoining the northwest and southeast sides of East State Highway 21 between North Earl Rudder Freeway (SH 6) and Old Kurten Road, North Thornberry Drive and Wallis Road, and at its intersection with Crosswind Drive. 

 Besides the 39 subject properties, a majority of properties along this corridor are currently zoned Industrial District (I), C-3 District, and RD-5 District. Additionally, there is a Planned Development – Industrial District (PD-I), being the Carrabba Industrial Park, as well as a Planned Development – Business District (PD-B), being Coulter Airfield. Planned Development Districts were not included in this assessment. The existing RD-5 District zoned properties not a part of this proposal are the Castle Heights Subdivision, a low-density residential development of approximately 450 lots. 

 The Commercial District (C-3) was selected as the desired zoning district in this area due to the recent and expected development trends and suitability along this corridor. Additionally, the majority of these properties are envisioned for commercial development by the City’s Comprehensive Plan (BluePrint 2040). The C-3 District is intended for heavy retail and commercial uses of a service nature, which typically have characteristics or traffic requirements generally compatible with typical retail or shopping, but generally not with residential environments. To note, any permitted use in either the Office District (C-1) or Retail District (C-2) also is permitted under C-3 District zoning, per Sections 130-14 and 130-15 of the Bryan Code of Ordinances. 

 On March 22, 2024, all tenants and property owners whose properties are considered for rezoning received written notification of the Planning and Zoning Commission’s proposal. To date, feedback and/or questions have been received via email and telephone regarding nineteen (19) of the subject properties. Five (5) of these properties are currently zoned Industrial District, which have since been removed from this request. The most frequent feedback received were concerns regarding the potential effect a rezoning might have on taxes for each property. Representatives of the Brazos County Appraisal District (BCAD) confirmed with staff that property taxes are not affected by zoning changes, and changes in tax rates or land values are only supported with a sufficient amount of evidence, which must be based on sales data. 

 Property owners also requested general information about C-3 zoning and the implications of the rezoning request, specifically the impact on existing uses of a property. Section 130-40(c)(1) of the Bryan Code of Ordinances allows for the existing lawful uses and structures to continue until the nonconforming use or structure is discontinued or abandoned. Thus, property owners and tenants of the subject properties are permitted to continue their current use until discontinuance or abandonment occurs. That is, only upon development or redevelopment of a property can these new regulations can be enforced. Of the 39 properties being proposed for rezoning, 23 are occupied by land uses permitted by right in the C-3 District. Of the 16 properties with land uses not permitted by-right, 15 are permitted with prior approval of a Conditional Use Permit from the Planning and Zoning Commission. 

 Analysis and Recommendation: 

 During the Planning and Zoning Commission’s public hearing on May 2, 2024, three (3) citizens spoke to express their concerns about the request, specifically how the proposed rezoning will affect the current and future uses of their properties. Following the public hearing, the Commission voted to recommend approval of the proposal, subject to the condition that properties zoned Industrial District (I) be removed. The motion passed by a vote of four (4) in favor and three (3) in opposition. The Commissioners in opposition to the motion wished not to remove the industrial properties from the proposal. 

 The Planning and Zoning Commission finds that: 

 The Commercial District (C-3) is compatible with the existing growth trends of the area and is consistent with the land use recommendations of the City’s Comprehensive Plan (BluePrint 2040), which provides this area as being most appropriate for commercial and regional retail uses. 

 East State Highway 21, a major arterial roadway as identified on the City’s thoroughfare plan, is capable of accommodating traffic loads typically associated with commercial development. The proposed zoning is appropriate on the subject properties as their location on a major arterial makes them ideal for commercial development. 

 The requested rezoning of the subject properties to Commercial District (C-3) will not make land classified for similar development in the vicinity and elsewhere in the City unavailable for development. 

 The intensification of zoning and permitted uses is appropriate for properties along East State Highway 21 currently zoned A-O District and RD-5 District. 

 The Commission finds changing the zoning of industrial properties to C-3 District is not appropriate at this location at this time due to potential impacts on subject properties and the concerns expressed by current owners of these properties. 

 Note: The draft ordinance attached to this Council Action Form excludes properties currently zoned Industrial District (I), as recommended by the Planning and Zoning Commission. 

 Options: 

 approve the requested zoning change with the modification recommended by P&Z; 

 approve the requested zoning change with modifications, which may require rescheduling the request for consideration on a future City Council meeting agenda; 

 deny the requested zoning change; or 

 deny the requested zoning change with prejudice, as provided for in Zoning Ordinance Section 130-42(i)(2): “If a request has been denied with prejudice, the same or similar request may not be resubmitted to the city for six months from the original date of denial.” 

 Attachments: 

 location map and aerial photographs; 

 draft ordinance with exhibits; 

 excerpt from February 1, March 7, and April 4, 2024, Planning and Zoning Commission workshop meeting minutes; 

 excerpt from May 2, 2024, Planning and Zoning Commission meeting minutes; 

 subject property owner/tenant feedback;

 correspondence with the Brazos county appraisal district regarding taxes; and

 Staff report to the Planning and Zoning Commission.

Public hearing, presentation and consideration of adoption of an ordinance on first and only reading to amend the text of Bryan Code of Ordinances Chapter 2 – Administration, Chapter 62 – Land and Site Development, Chapter 110 – Subdivisions and Chapter 130 – Zoning, by removing references to the Planning and Zoning Commission’s platting authority and providing the Site Development Review Committee (SDRC) with platting approval authority

 Summary: 

 House Bill 3699, relating to municipal regulation of subdivisions and approval of subdivision plans and plat approval, was adopted and signed by the Governor on June 18, 2023, during the 88th regular session of the Texas Legislature. One of the elements of this bill expanded the ability to delegate platting authority to the staff level. 

 The City of Bryan’s platting procedure is defined and regulated by Chapter 110, Subdivisions. Currently, plats involving more than four lots or the construction of public infrastructure require approval from the Planning and Zoning Commission. City staff, and specifically the SDRC chair, has the authority to approve minor plats (less than four lots with existing access to public infrastructure) and preliminary plans. If approved, this text amendment will delegate all platting authority to City staff, unless otherwise requested by the applicant or by staff. 

 Delegating platting authority to staff will expedite the time required for plat approval, potentially saving time and costs for customers. Staff time will be saved and allocated elsewhere in the absence of preparing associated staff reports and maps. Additionally, the number of Planning and Zoning Commission meetings may be reduced and/or time spent in Commission meetings may be reduced. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 

 During their regular meeting on June 20, 2024, the Planning and Zoning Commission voted to recommend approval of the proposed amendment to the text of Bryan Code of Ordinances Chapter 2 – Administration, Chapter 62 – Land and Site Development, Chapter 110 – Subdivisions and Chapter 130 – Zoning, to remove references to the Planning and Zoning Commission’s platting authority and providing the Site Development Review Committee (SDRC) with platting approval authority. The motion passed by a vote of five (5) in favor and three (3) in opposition. 

 Delegating platting authority to staff has the ability to expedite and streamline the development process, thereby enhancing customer service; 

 Delegating platting authority to staff can relieve staff of preparing detailed reports and reduce the number of potential Planning and Zoning Commission meetings. 

 Options: 

 approve Bryan Code of Ordinances text amendment, as recommended by P&Z; 

 approve Bryan Code of Ordinances text amendment with modifications (which may require City Council consideration at a future City Council meeting); or 

 not approve this Bryan Code of Ordinances text amendment at this time and provide direction to staff. 

 Attachments: 

 draft ordinance; 

 excerpt from May 16, 2024, and June 20, 2024, Planning and Zoning Commission meeting minutes; and 

 memorandum to the Planning and Zoning Commission.

 Type

 Goals

 Summary: 
 On December 3, 2024, Request for Proposal (RFP) #25-007 (Fueling Center Reconstruction at Municipal Service Center) was opened for the reconstruction of the Waco Street Fuel Island. The City received one proposal submitted by A1 Pump Inc. of Bryan, TX in the not to exceed amount of $1,339,384.08. 

 This project will provide regulatory closure of the existing fuel island with the reconstruction at a new location within the Municipal Service Center (MSC). Fuel storage capacity will be increased from 24,000 gallons of diesel and 12,000 gallons of unleaded gasoline to 30,000 gallons of each fuel type with the addition of 1,200 gallons of Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) added for dispensing. Increasing tank size adds available storage and streamlines fuel delivery by providing opportunities to accept complete transports (8,000 gallons) instead of split compartment deliveries as a result of the wider operating tolerance of the higher volume tanks. 

 The fuel management software and dispensing equipment will be upgraded to a new platform (GasBoy). Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology will replace chip keys and the 9-pin encoder used for activation of the island terminal. The chip key system is problematic and a fading technology that will be replaced by a key fob and reader. The new management software is web-based instead of locally installed. The field island terminal and ancillary equipment will use its own dedicated wireless network to communicate with Gasboy's server. This approach fully isolates the fuel island from the City's network and is value added for cybersecurity. The wireless network will allow Gasboy the ability to perform remote troubleshooting and maintenance of the fuel island and fuel management software. 

 The island terminal is conditioned to activate only when its rules have been met: (1) upon driver identification authorized for fuel access, and (2) when vehicle identification is authorized for fuel access. In this process, the driver inputs the vehicle's mileage/hours and fuel type requested into the island terminal. A feature of the new system is an opportunity to automate the authorization process. Under this approach, no change will occur with driver identification; however, all fuel dispensers will be outfitted with RFID technology, which activates when the fuel nozzle is inserted into the fuel inlet of a RFID-equipped vehicle (ex: tank ring or tag). Communication between the fuel nozzle and a programmed tank ring or tag activates the pump and omits the need for vehicle identification to be physically entered into the island terminal. The fuel type, frequency, and maximum volume (daily or per transaction) established for the vehicle is programmed into the tank ring or tag to further eliminate human error or theft. Removing the nozzle from the vehicle's fuel inlet immediately suspends fueling activity. Tank rings and tags are designed to lose function if tampered with or removed from an equipped vehicle. 

 Going a step further with automation, the system is able to tap into the vehicle's On-Board Diagnostics (ODB) to automatically pull the vehicle’s odometer (mileage or engine hours), GPS location of the vehicle, engine diagnostics, and warning lights. A monthly service fee per equipped vehicle is required for this service. The contract presented before the City Council provides licensing and equipment for a pilot study of the ODB service using selected solid waste collection vehicles to determine if the cost-benefit of the ODB option warrants further expansion into the fleet. 

 Demolition and regulatory closure of the original fuel island is a deliverable for this contract. Through this process, removal and disposal of the underground storage tanks and product lines will be performed. The contractor will coordinate regulatory closure of the site with the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) in accordance with its requirements. 

 This project is an approved Decision Package for FY2023 ($1,500,000). Professional services for design of this project were expensed at $113,900. The construction contract presented for consideration places the complete project inline with the funded Decision Package. Expenses for this project will be split funded between the Enterprise and General Fund. Funding levels were established from system use, with the following allocations: Wastewater Fund 9.1%, Water Fund 7.9%, Solid Waste 36.2%, and General Fund 46.8%. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Water Services recommends the City Council award contract to A1 Pump Inc. in the not to exceed amount of $1,339,384.08 allowing for construction of the Waco Street Fuel Island and regulatory closure of the preceding. 

 Options: 
 1. Approve purchase 
 2. Do not approve purchase and provide direction

 1. Contract 
 2. Fuel Island Drawings

 Summary: 
 On November 15, 2022, the City of Bryan entered into a Ground Lease Agreement with SMBG Bryan, LLC for 5.644 acres in Travis Bryan Midtown Park for development of a multiuse sports/recreation/entertainment facility along the southwest shore of Midtown Lake near the intersection of West Villa Maria Road and South College Avenue. The facility is currently under construction to include indoor and outdoor non-shooting target sports, bowling, darts, axe throwing, bocce ball, shuffle board, indoor and outdoor pickleball, technology advanced auditoriums allowing motion pictures/movies, live event broadcasts, e-sports, conference space, arcade, outdoor amphitheater, and supplementary food and beverage services.

 Under the Ground Lease, the City of Bryan as Landlord is required to provide utilities to the leased area, construct “Road A”, provide a minimum of 250 non-exclusive public parking spaces in proximity to the facility, and allow at least two (2) points of access between the leased area and a future public boardwalk, to be constructed by the City of Bryan along the shoreline of Midtown Lake. The Ground Lease term is thirty (30) years with two (2) renewal options for ten (10) years each, with escalating rental payments for use of the leased area due to the City as per the Ground Lease Agreement.

 A First Amendment to the Ground Lease Agreement was approved on July 11, 2023 to modify certain Tenant deadlines. On January 23, 2024, the City Council gave consent to grant security interests to allow SMBG to enter into a builder and mechanic’s lien contract for Bartlett Cocke General Contractors, LLC to begin construction of the facility.

 This proposed Chapter 380 Agreement provides for a grant in the form of a Chapter 380 loan to SMBG Bryan, LLC in the amount of $2,000,000 to be repaid no later than two years from its funding to continue uninterrupted construction of the Project, and to enhance certain terms included in the original Ground Lease Agreement.

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Staff recommends approval of this Chapter 380 Agreement, which assists in the timely development of the Project. The proposed Agreement requires an amendment to the Ground Lease Agreement to increase the minimum taxable appraised value of the Project from $19 million to $24 million, to establish a minimum construction investment of $37 million, and to provide for additional enhancements to the pickleball courts, outdoor amphitheater, stage, small playground, restrooms, and food and beverage cantina. Timely completion of the Project will in turn expand the ad valorem and sales tax base, create jobs, stimulate business and commercial activity, and spur economic development in the City of Bryan.

 Summary: 
 The City of Bryan has General Liability, Law Enforcement Liability, Errors & Omissions Liability and Auto Liability with the Texas Municipal League Intergovernmental Risk Pool (TMLIRP). These coverages are being considered in a separate action form. This Council Action Form seeks to award Excess General Liability and Auto Liability coverage for Bryan Texas Utilities (BTU) specific exposures. The current liability policy through TMLIRP has a $500,000 deductible and provides various limits. That is, if a claim exceeds $500,000, TMLIRP will cover $2,000,000 per occurrence/$6,000,000 aggregate for General Liability, $3,000,000 per occurrence/$6,000,000 aggregate for Law Enforcement Liability, and $2,000,000 per occurrence/$4,000,000 aggregate for Errors & Omissions Liability. The proposed coverage is a new policy. This policy will be in excess of the TMLIRP policy limits (for BTU-related exposures only), and will provide an additional $5,000,000 per occurrence under General Liability for a total of $7,000,00 per occurrence between both policies, and an additional $5,000,000 under Auto Liability for a total of $8,000,000 per occurrence. The proposed policy has a wildfire exclusion, and is intended to cover only the utility operations, not other exposures such as police and fire. The total premium for the proposed coverage is $230,758.

 The average gross incurred excess liability by the recommended carrier, AEGIS, year over year (excluding wildfire claims) has increased from approximately $3.5M in 2015 to upwards of $7.5M in 2023. AEGIS is a mutual insurer formed in 1986 by utilities when the commercial marketplace stopped providing the capacity and coverage terms meeting the needs of utilities. Nuclear verdicts and catastrophic risk exposures within utilities as well as their proprietary function status, solidify the need for additional coverage for Bryan Texas Utilities. In addition, this proposed policy provides TRIA coverage. The Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA) of 2002 provides a temporary federal program for compensating insured losses from certified acts of terrorism. Typically this coverage costs an additional $5,000; however, AEGIS has agreed to include it within their premium. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 The City's Sole Broker of Record did an extensive market check and along with City staff, reviewed various options including higher limits. The proposed coverage will provide additional coverage for BTU-related exposures and provide a degree of financial protection in the event of a catastrophic loss. 

 Staff respectfully recommends award of Excess Liability Insurance with a $5,000,000 limit for BTU-related exposures at an annual premium of $230,758 for the policy period beginning October 1, 2024, and ending September 30, 2025. 

 Options: 
 Award Excess Liability Coverage for utility related exposures to AEGIS at annual premium of $230,758 for the FY2025 policy period.
 Do not award the Excess Liability Coverage for utility related exposures to AEGIS and require staff to request additional proposals. Note: this will require action at a future Council meeting. 
 Do not award the Excess Liability Coverage for utility related exposures to AEGIS and provide direction to staff. Note: not awarding the policy could increase BTU's financial exposure.

 Summary: 
 Destination Bryan (DB) is a nonprofit organization established in 2020 to serve as Bryan's own destination marketing organization (DMO), and was recognized in 2022 as DMO of the Year for the State of Texas. DB is tasked with telling Bryan's story, while offering unique experiences to its visitors. DB also is responsible for coordinating with local entities to attract large-scale events and groups that collectively fill Bryan's hotels, use facilities, and power economic growth.

 The proposed DB Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 Budget was recommended for approval by the DB Board, which includes members Spencer Clements, Andrew Nelson, and Kindra Fry, and is consistent with direction received at the June 18, 2024, Bryan City Council Workshop. DB's FY2025 request includes $2,950,000 in operational funding, inclusive of $2,470,000 in Hotel Occupancy Tax (HOT) funds, and $480,000 in General Funds. Use of General Funds allows DB to operate and promote events that impact quality of life and the local economy, which indirectly boosts the tourism economy as well. The total amount from the City of Bryan represents an increase of 6.69 percent over FY2024 ($2,765,000). The increased funding in FY2025 is for additional costs associated with administration, content creation, increased advertising, and new events.

 The DB Budget for FY2025 is attached as an exhibit to the Resolution, with total revenues in the amount of $3,191,150 and total expenses in the amount of $3,191,150. While City of Bryan HOT collections were limited in Fiscal Years 2020 and 2021 due to COVID-19 impacts on the hotel industry, Bryan's HOT Fund collections continue to recover. HOT collections are forecast to exceed $2.4 million by the end of FY2024.

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Staff recommends approving this Resolution and FY2025 funding agreement for DB. In just four years of existence, DB is now an award-winning destination marketing organization (DMO) recognized among its peers throughout the state of Texas. DB continues to expand its range of services with targeted, strategic, and effective destination marketing efforts, which are essential to growth in the Bryan hospitality and tourism industry. 

 This funding agreement is consistent with direction received from City Council to expand DB's services and marketing appeal, while also managing, operating, and promoting events of all kinds, and administering the Event-Based Hotel Occupancy Tax (HOT) Grant Program.

 Summary: 
 In January 2020, the City entered into a design contract with Walker Partners to design the west side sewer improvements, which includes gravity sewer lines, a lift station, and a force main. The purpose of this contract was to provide sewer service access along the SH47 corridor. The infrastructure in the design contract serves as the major infrastructure for this area of Bryan from which future extensions will serve additional property. In February 2023, the City Council authorized the purchase of 1.5 acres out of a tract of land located at the end of Bush Lane. The 1.5 acre tract is the location of the proposed lift station in this construction contract. 

 The lift station site is designed to have room for expansion for up to two additional wet wells. This first phase will be capable of moving up to 3 MGD of wastewater. Some piping is included in this project for the second phase of the improvements in this area to connect to the lift station (gravity line and force main). The second phase is currently advertised for bid. 

 This project was advertised for bid on July 23, 2024. Competitive sealed proposals were received on August 15, 2024; one responsive bid was received. The engineer's estimate for the project was $4.1 million. The responsive bid is approximately $1.5 million more than the engineer's estimate. An inquiry from the design engineer to other potential bidders found the work was either too small for larger contractors to mobilize to the area or too large for some of the local contractors to consider. References for Horton Excavating, LLC were checked and their references came back with glowing remarks on their quality of work. The contract allows for 200 working days to complete the work. 

 This work will be paid for from the American Rescue Plan Act funds and was budgeted to come from this funding source. As a reminder, the funds under this funding source need to be under contract by the end of calendar year 2024. Since this was a competitive sealed proposal, staff has inquired with the contractor on cost savings. Initially there appears to be at least $100,000 in savings. Staff recommends, if the City Council awards this contract, allowing staff to investigate other cost saving measures with the vendor prior to equipment being ordered. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 Staff recommends awarding the construction contract to Horton Excavating, LLC. This lift station will serve as the major component to providing wastewater in west Bryan along the State Highway 47 corridor.

 Summary: 
 In April 2013, as part of an economic development incentive package to help locate an industrial manufacturing plant on property in the Texas Triangle Industrial Park, the City of Bryan and Kuadrum Pipe and Tube Inc., now known as Axis Pipe and Tube Inc., entered into a non-annexation agreement pursuant to Chapter 212 of the Texas Local Government Code. The purpose of this non-annexation agreement was to guarantee the continuation of the extraterritorial status of the property and its immunity from annexation by the municipality for a period of ten (10) years. As part of the agreement, attached as Exhibit “3”, City of Bryan police and fire protection and access to City water lines were provided to the property. In exchange, the company agreed to add at least $120 million in taxable value, employ at least 285 full-time employees, and maintain an agreed-upon aggregate gross salary base. The 10-year term expired on December 31, 2023, which per the agreement, constituted a petition for annexation into the City limits.

The property owner requests the subject property be assigned Planned Development – Industrial District (PD-I) zoning upon annexation. The PD-I District allows all land uses allowed in the City’s Industrial zoning district, except adult entertainment uses. The requested zoning district is consistent with the existing zoning districts within the Texas Triangle Industrial Park.

State law requires the annexation ordinance include a municipal service plan that details the specific municipal services to be provided to the area after it has been annexed. Staff anticipates no extraordinary new services, facilities, or expenses as a result of this annexation. Domestic water supply and sanitary sewer service will continue to be provided by the City of Bryan. A copy of this service agreement is attached to this Council Action Form.

 Analysis and Recommendation: 
 During its regular meeting on September 5, 2024, the Planning and Zoning Commission concurred with staff and unanimously voted to recommend approval of the owner-requested annexation of these 182.73 acres, and to assign Planned Development – Industrial District (PD-I) zoning to the property upon annexation. The Commission adopted the written staff report and analysis as the report, findings, and evaluation of the Commission.

 Approving the requested annexation will bring 182.73 acres of land under the full regulatory control of the City; annexation of this acreage can, therefore, help promote orderly urban growth in the Texas Triangle Industrial Park area. 
 The Planning and Zoning Commission anticipates no extraordinary new services, facilities, or expenses as a result of this annexation. 
 The Planning and Zoning Commission contends that that the proposed PD-I zoning district is most appropriate and efficient for the land in this specific case. 
 Assigning PD-I District accommodates the manufacturing and office/warehouse uses.

 Options: 
 approve the proposed owner-initiated annexation; or
 approve the proposed owner-initiated annexation with modifications, which may require rescheduling the request for consideration on a future City Council meeting agenda, re-notification and/or newspaper publication; or
 do not approve this proposed owner-initiated annexation at this time and provide direction to staff.

 location maps;
 draft annexation ordinance and exhibits with service plan; 
 excerpt from September 5, 2024 Planning and Zoning Commission regular meeting minutes;
 staff report to the Planning and Zoning Commission; and 
 attachments to staff report to the Planning and Zoning Commission.

 Summary: 
 In 2016, the City Council adopted the City of Bryan Financial Management Policy Statements (FMPS). These statements were designed to assemble the City’s major financial policies into one document. The statements are a tool used to ensure the City is financially able to meet its current and future service needs. 

 The stated objectives of the FMPS are: 
 To guide the City Council and management policy decisions that have significant fiscal impact. 
 To employ balanced revenue policies that provide adequate funding for services and service levels. 
 To maintain appropriate financial capacity for present and future needs. 
 To maintain sufficient reserves to maintain service levels during periods of economic downturn. 
 To promote sound financial management by providing accurate and timely information on the City’s financial condition. 
 To protect the City’s credit rating and provide for adequate resources to meet the provisions of the City’s debt obligations on all municipal debt. 
 To ensure the legal use of financial resources through an effective system of internal controls. 
 To enhance transparency in financial matters. 
 Included in the FMPS is a biennial requirement to review and update, if needed, any of the FMPS to better reflect statutory requirements or any change in policy. 

 In January 2018, the City Council amended the FMPS updating reporting requirements as well as the required and target ending balances for specific funds. The amendment also included several housekeeping items intended to make the document easier to read (e.g., formatting, clarification, etc.). 

 In January 2020, the City Council amended the FMPS updating several items with regard to the approval and selection of the City's external auditor, lien collection practices, target unrestricted cash for various funds, and specific debt coverage matrices for BTU City and Rural. 

 In September 2020, the City Council amended the FMPS updating the sections on Debt Financing, Debt Structures, and Use of Debt Financing to accommodate the issuance and debt schedules of the City's General Obligation Pension Bonds, Series 2020. This amendment also included several housekeeping items intended to clarify the intent of certain sections of the document. 

 In November 2021, the City Council amended the FMPS updating target unrestricted cash for BTU City, BTU Rural, and the Employee Benefits Fund. This amendment also included several housekeeping items intended to clarify the intent of certain sections of the document. 

 Staff recommends the following changes to the City's FMPS: 

 Sections: I.A & I.D – Updated annual report name from Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) to Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR). The name changed effective March 9, 2021. 
 Section: I.E – Added language to specify check signers for management companies. 
 Section: III.1.c – Added certificates of obligation, since it’s a commonly used debt instrument. 
 Section: III.I.3 – Deleted section in its entirety, since the Distinguished Budget Presentation Award is not actively pursued. 
 Sections: IV.A.1 & IV.A.3 – Clarified language related to property taxes transferred to Enterprise and Oil & Gas funds. 
 Section: V.A – Updated capitalization threshold from $5,000 and one year useful life to $10,000 and three year useful life. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 At the September 12, 2024, Audit Committee meeting, the Audit Committee unanimously recommended approving the Policy amendments. Staff also recommends approving the changes outlined above. 

 Options: 
 Adopt policy amendments as proposed 
 Adopt a portion of the policy amendments as proposed, which may require consideration at a future City Council meeting 
 Do not adopt the policy amendments as proposed and provide direction to staff

Staff anticipates no extraordinary new services, facilities, or expenses as a result of this annexation. Domestic water supply and sanitary sewer service will be provided by the City. A copy of the service agreement is attached to this Council Action Form.

 Analysis and Recommendation: 
 During its regular meeting on October 3, 2024, the Planning and Zoning Commission concurred with staff and unanimously voted to recommend approval of the owner-requested annexation of these 41.46 acres, and to assign Planned Development – Industrial District (PD-I) zoning to the property upon annexation. The Commission adopted the written staff report and analysis as the report, findings, and evaluation of the Commission.

 Approving the requested annexation will bring 41.46 acres of land under the full regulatory control of the City; annexation of this acreage can, therefore, help promote orderly urban growth in the Texas Triangle Industrial Park area. 
 The Planning and Zoning Commission anticipates no extraordinary new services, facilities, or expenses as a result of this annexation. 
 The Planning and Zoning Commission contends the proposed PD-I zoning district is most appropriate and efficient for the land in this specific case. 

 Options: 
 approve the proposed owner-initiated annexation; or
 approve the proposed owner-initiated annexation with modifications, which may require rescheduling the request for consideration on a future City Council meeting agenda, re-notification and/or newspaper publication; or
 do not approve this proposed owner-initiated annexation at this time and provide direction to staff.

 Attachments: 
 location maps;
 draft annexation ordinance and exhibits with service plan; 
 excerpt from October 3, 2024, Planning and Zoning Commission regular meeting minutes;
 staff report to the Planning and Zoning Commission; and 
 attachments to staff report to the Planning and Zoning Commission.

matters.title: G. Approval of a Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with Bryan Commerce and Development (BCD) to authorize the conveyance of certain rights-of-way on the north end of Downtown Bryan and further approval of a Chapter 380 Economic Development agreement with OFL Group LTD CO to develop a hotel,
matters.body: Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting
matters.text:
Agenda Item Details 

 Meeting 
 Nov 12, 2024 - Bryan City Council Second Regular Meeting 
 Category 
 6. Statutory (Automatic Approval) Agenda - This agenda consists of items previously approved by Council action such as adoption of items that are part of an approved budget or capital improvement projects, first and only readings of ordinances, interlocal agreements, or action that is required by law or delegated to the City Manager. Items may be removed from the statutory agenda for separate consideration at the request of two Councilmembers. 
 Subject 
 G. Approval of a Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with Bryan Commerce and Development (BCD) to authorize the conveyance of certain rights-of-way on the north end of Downtown Bryan and further approval of a Chapter 380 Economic Development agreement with OFL Group LTD CO to develop a hotel, two multi story multi-purpose structures and associated parking structures, and other public infrastructure 
 Type 
 Action (Statutory) 
 Preferred Date 
 Nov 12, 2024 
 Absolute Date 
 Nov 12, 2024 
 Fiscal Impact 
 Yes 
 Dollar Amount 
 17,000,000.00 
 Budgeted 
 No 
 Budget Source 
 Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone #21, Hotel Occupancy Tax Fund, and General Fund 
 Goals 

 Quality of Life 

 Infrastructure 

 Economic Development 

 Summary: 
 Bryan Commerce and Development (BCD) owns approximately four (4) acres of land on the north end of Downtown Bryan, generally defined as Blocks 105, 106, 260 (lots 1-3), and 123 (lots 3R - 6R) of the Bryan Original Townsite. In 2022, BCD issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) seeking a development partnership to complete the development of this critical northern gateway into the core of Downtown. BCD, in concert with the City of Bryan, was seeking a public-private partnership that would have significant economic, social, and cultural impact on the community. As a result of the RFP, BCD and the City of Bryan entered into negotiations with OFL Group of Bryan, Texas to develop plans for a multi-phase, mixed-use, high-density development.

 OFL Group is ready to embark on a transformative 3-phase development, completing the restoration of Downtown to its historic grandeur, while paving the way for a vibrant future. The developer plans to break ground in 2025 on Phase I, featuring a five-story, 130-room upscale hotel under a prominent flag, integrated with a modern conference center and a parking structure for at least 340 vehicles. Construction is projected to finish by 2027.

 Phase II, scheduled for completion in 2029, will introduce a six-story, mixed-use residential building, on top of an underground parking facility for approximately 400 vehicles, enhancing both urban living and accessibility.

 Phase III will add another six-story, multi-use structure, attracting new residents to the heart of Downtown. If market conditions align, this phase may include condominium units and an office component, supporting long-term community stability and fostering ownership within the district.

 This property is currently located within Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone (TIRZ) #21. The increased taxable value of all properties in this zone must be reinvested back into the area through approved projects. Through a unique partnership between the City of Bryan, Brazos County, and OFL Group, the taxable value generated from this development will be used to participate in the construction of at least 300 publicly available parking spaces in Downtown North, as well as vital infrastructure to support the development. The parking and infrastructure is being financed and built by the private-sector and reimbursed by the TIRZ only when the forecasted increase in taxable values and other benchmarks have been achieved.

 To maximize the limited land area available and encourage a denser land use with adequate off-street parking, all while promoting a walkable and pedestrian friendly environment, the City of Bryan is pursuing the closure of portions of Bryan Avenue, and a portion of East Pruitt Street and West 21st Street directly adjacent to the subject properties. The Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with BCD will authorize the applicable rights-of-way to be closed and conveyed to the developer through BCD. There will be an additional companion item on the BCD agenda to address the ground lease and future conveyance of the subject property to OFL Group.

 The Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with OFL Group is a performance-based agreement that outlines the expectations for land use, density, increased taxable value, and timelines. The agreement also contains a recapture provision in the event certain benchmarks are not met.

 In general terms, the Developer agrees to:

 Construct a flagged hotel with at least 130 rooms, a conference space with at least 12,000 square feet of meeting space, and a parking structure with at least 340 parking spaces in Phase I of the Project (Phase I). Construction for Phase I must begin prior to December 31, 2025. The developer must receive a certificate of occupancy (CO) for all structures in Phase I by December 31, 2027. 
 Construct a multi-story mixed use building of at least six (6) stories in height, with at least 40,000 square feet of leasable space, with restaurant and retail space on the first floor, and office, retail, restaurant, and/or residences on the remaining floors and an underground parking structure with 400 spaces (Phase II). Phase II construction must begin prior to January 1, 2028. The developer must receive a CO for Phase II by December 1, 2029. 
 Before obtaining a CO for Phase I, convey to the City a non-exclusive easement for the benefit of the public, permitting the use of at least 150 parking spaces in the Phase I parking structure. On or before obtaining a CO for Phase II, convey to the City a non-exclusive easement for the benefit of the public, permitting the use of at least 150 of the underground parking spaces in Phase II. 
 Construct a second multi-story, mixed-use building with a minimum height of six (6) stories and at least 60,000 square feet of space. The first floor must feature leasable or purchasable retail, office, or restaurant spaces. The upper floors may include a combination of office, retail, restaurant, or residential units. Additionally, public infrastructure improvements must be provided to meet the needs of the property, including but not limited to publicly accessible green spaces, walkways, irrigation systems, and lighting (Phase III). Phase III construction must begin prior to January 1, 2030, with the developer obtaining a CO for the building by July 1, 2031.
 Phase I of the Project will be appraised by Brazos Central Appraisal District (BCAD) at a taxable value of at least $38,000,000 by tax year 2028 and through the end of the Agreement.
 Phase II of the Project will be appraised by BCAD at a taxable value of at least $48,000,000 by tax year 2030 and through the end of the Agreement.
 Phase III of the Project will be appraised by BCAD at a taxable value of at least $40,000,000 by tax year 2032 and through the end of the Agreement.
 Comply with all recapture provisions should they fail to satisfy the required benchmarks.

 In general terms, the City agrees to:

 Close portions of Bryan Avenue (from 22nd Street to Martin Luther King, Jr. Street), Pruitt Street (from Main Street to Bryan Avenue) and 21st Street (from Main Street to Bryan Avenue) and convey to the developer through BCD. 

 Waive up to $100,000 (in the aggregate) in permit fees.
 Rebate fifty percent (50%) of all Hotel Occupancy Tax (HOT) fund revenue generated by the hotel in Phase I, not to exceed $2,250,000. 
 Create an Infrastructure Grant Fund, through the Board of Directors of Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone (TIRZ) #21, and sequester one hundred percent (100%) of the tax increment generated by Phases I and II, as well as the unencumbered portion of the remaining tax increment generated by TIRZ #21.
 Make bi-annual grant payments from the Infrastructure Grant Fund up to $8,500,000 in the aggregate for Phase I, up to $4,000,000 in the aggregate for Phase II, and up to $1,500,000 in the aggregate for Phase III for costs associated with infrastructure including publicly accessible above ground structure and underground parking, parks and play areas, updates to existing roadways, updates to and construction of sidewalks and pathways, landscaping, lighting, and upgrades to and/or relocation of electrical lines, water lines, sewer lines, and storm sewer currently located within the public right-of-way.
 Provide a density bonus in the form of additional Infrastructure Grant payments if the developer elects to increase the height of the building(s) to at least ten (10) stories in Phase II and/or Phase III, and if the combined BCAD value of the structures on Phases II and III exceeds $110,000,000. 

 Staff Analysis and Recommendation: 
 BCD and the City of Bryan issued a Request for Proposals to identify and secure a world-class private sector development partner for the redevelopment of Downtown North property. This development proposal captures the vision of the Downtown North property as an experiential destination, a magnet and catalyst for residents and visitors alike anchoring Downtown Bryan’s northern gateway. Based upon the agreement terms, the following fiscal impacts are projected over the next 25 years:

 Land sell at approximately $2,100,000;
 City sales tax estimated at $510,075 annually; and
 City Hotel Occupancy Tax estimated at $635,645 annually.

 Beyond the fiscal impacts referenced above, staff believes this project will have significant indirect/spin-off benefits serving as a catalyst for the continued renaissance of Bryan’s Historic Downtown. Staff recommends approval of this public-private partnership redevelopment initiative that brings significant economic and social impact, while retaining Downtown Bryan’s unique Cultural District position in the market.

 Options: 
 1. Approve both Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreements
 2. Deny both Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreements and provide direction to staff 

 Attachments: 
 1. Subject property map
 2. Downtown North RFP
 3. Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with BCD 
 4. Chapter 380 Economic Development Agreement with OFL Group
